old: Modals (vouloir, pouvoir, devoir) take the infinitive directly. je veux manger (I want to eat), il peut aider (he can help). No preposition between them.
focus: vouloir/pouvoir take the bare infinitive with no preposition – anchor to 'veut partir' itself, drop the verb-list lead

old: Ouvrir (to open) is irregular: j'ouvre, tu ouvres, il ouvre, nous ouvrons. Despite being -ir, it uses -er endings in present.
focus: ouvrir looks like an -ir verb but takes -er endings in the present – keep that surprise, cut the paradigm list, anchor 'j'ouvre'

old: 'Regarder' means 'to watch/look at' – the 'at' is built in. No preposition needed: je regarde la télé, not *je regarde à la télé.
focus: regarder has 'at' built in, no preposition – remove the asterisk ungrammaticality marker, anchor 'regardez la télévision'

old: 'Adorer' = to love/adore. Stronger than 'aimer'. With general nouns, use the article: 'adorent le chocolat'.
focus: adorer = love vs aimer = like for things – one rule only, cut the article clause (covered on fr-0027), anchor 'adorent le chocolat'

target: Il passe ses vacances à Nice.
english: He spends his holidays in Nice.
old: 'Passer' = to spend (time). With places, use `à` for cities: 'à Paris', 'à Nice'.
focus: passer = to spend time ('passe ses vacances') – remove backticks, cut the à-for-cities second rule (covered on fr-0042)

old: Aimer is a regular -er verb. Use aimer + definite article for general likes: J'aime le café (I like coffee in general).
focus: definite article for general likes ('aimez le café') where English uses bare noun – cut the 'regular -er verb' filler clause

old: Partitive articles `du/de la/des` = 'some' (unspecified quantity). `Je mange du pain` = 'I eat some bread'. English often drops 'some'; French keeps the article.
focus: des = 'some' that English drops – remove backticks, replace the du pain example with this card's 'prend des photos'

old: With numbers, no article before the noun: 'deux enfants', not *'deux des enfants'. The number replaces the article.
focus: a number replaces the article ('deux enfants', never 'deux des enfants') – remove the asterisk marker, keep it one rule

old: `vous` is both 'you (plural)' and 'you (formal singular)'. Context decides. With strangers, in business, or with older people → vous. With friends, family, kids → tu.
focus: tu vs vous stakes, anchored to 'Vous pouvez répéter ?' as the safe-with-strangers form – remove backticks, trim

old: Vouloir (to want) is irregular: je veux, tu veux, il veut, nous voulons, vous voulez, ils veulent. 'Je voudrais' is more polite.
focus: 'je veux un café' is blunt when ordering – 'je voudrais' is the polite ask; cut the vouloir paradigm entirely

old: Connaître (to know/be familiar with) is irregular: je connais, tu connais, il connaît, nous connaissons. Use for people/places/things.
focus: connaître = familiarity-knowing (people, places, songs) vs savoir = facts/how-to – cut the paradigm, anchor 'connais cette chanson'

old: 'Obéir à' = to obey. Regular -ir verb with -iss- in plural. Requires 'à': 'il obéit à ses parents'.
focus: obéir needs à where English takes a direct object ('obéit à ses parents') – cut the -iss-plural conjugation clause

old: 'Entrer dans' = to enter. Requires 'dans': 'vous entrez dans le magasin'. Uses 'être' in passé composé.
focus: entrer needs dans where English enters the store directly ('entrez dans le magasin') – cut the passé-composé être clause

old: 'Pouvoir' + infinitive = can/able to. 'Tu peux venir?' = Can you come? Informal question via intonation.
focus: Questions by intonation alone – 'Tu peux venir ?' keeps statement word order, no inversion needed in speech; cut the pouvoir+infinitive gloss.

old: Vouvoyer = use `vous`. Tutoyer = use `tu`. Wrong tu can be rude; wrong vous is just safe. When unsure, start formal and let them say `on peut se tutoyer`.
focus: tu/vous register stakes are real and anchored in this card's 'vous' – strip the backticks and keep the 'when unsure go formal' advice.

old: 'Aller à' = to go to. 'Au' = à+le: 'vous allez au marché' = you go to the market.
focus: au = à + le contraction, anchored in 'au marché' – cut the 'aller à' gloss and the full-sentence re-translation.

old: `on` is the all-purpose informal 'we' in spoken French: `on va au cinéma` = 'we're going to the movies' (not `nous`). Verbs conjugate as 3rd singular even though it means 'we'.
focus: on = spoken French's everyday 'we' taking a 3rd-singular verb – anchor to this card's 'On va', strip backticks, trim to target length.

english: I'm looking for the train station.
old: 'Chercher' means 'to look for' – the 'for' is built in. Say 'je cherche la gare', not *je cherche pour la gare.
focus: chercher has 'for' built in – never 'chercher pour'; keep the trap, remove the asterisk ungrammaticality notation.

old: 'Réfléchir à' = to think about. Regular -ir with -iss-. Requires 'à': 'je réfléchis à la question'.
focus: réfléchir à = think ABOUT – the à is required and anchored in 'à la question'; drop the -iss- conjugation note.

target: On fait les courses le samedi.
english: We do the shopping on Saturdays.
old: `on` also = English 'one' or 'they' (impersonal): `on dit que...` = 'they say that...'. Two meanings, one word. Context decides.
focus: on's second life as impersonal 'one/they' (on dit que) – a two-meanings landmine; strip backticks and anchor to this card's 'On fait'.

old: 'Venir de + infinitive' means 'to have just done something': je viens de manger = I just ate.
focus: venir de + infinitive = 'just did' – anchor in THIS card's 'venons de finir' (we just finished), not a sibling example

old: Venir (to come) is irregular: je viens, tu viens, il vient, nous venons, vous venez, ils viennent. 'Venir de' = to come from.
focus: venir de Lyon = origin, but venir de + verb = 'just did' – same phrase, two meanings, context decides; cut the conjugation table

old: Sortir (to go out) is irregular like partir: je sors, tu sors, il sort, nous sortons. Don't confuse with 'quitter' (to leave a place).
focus: English 'leave/go out' splits: sortir (je sors ce soir) vs quitter (leave a place) – lead with the split, drop the conjugation list

old: Use 'avoir' for physical features: avoir les cheveux bruns (to have brown hair), avoir les yeux verts (to have green eyes).
focus: the real trap is the definite article: elle a LES yeux bleus (the blue eyes), never 'des' – avoir itself matches English 'has' and needs no tip

old: je → j' before a vowel or silent h: j'aime (I love), j'habite (I live). Elision is mandatory – je aime is wrong.
focus: refocus on this card's real trap: age uses avoir – j'ai vingt-cinq ans = literally 'I have twenty-five years'; the generic elision rule isn't anchored here

old: Aller (to go) is irregular: je vais, tu vas, il/elle va, nous allons, vous allez, ils/elles vont. 'Au' = à + le (contraction).
focus: keep only the contraction: au = à + le (je vais au cinéma) – 'à le' never exists; cut the aller conjugation table

old: 'Beau/belle' is one of the BANGS adjectives that go before the noun: 'une belle maison', not *'une maison belle'.
focus: belle goes BEFORE the noun (une belle maison) – short common adjectives precede; remove the literal asterisk and the unexplained BANGS acronym

old: Suivre (to follow) is irregular: je suis, tu suis, il suit, nous suivons, vous suivez, ils suivent. Same 'je suis' as être – context decides.
focus: je suis = 'I am' (être) AND 'I follow' (suivre) – here it's following the lesson; keep only this landmine, cut the conjugation table

english: An hour is enough for me.
old: 'Il me suffit de' = it suffices for me / is enough for me. Same reverse pattern: il te suffit de, il lui suffit de.
focus: il me suffit d'une heure = 'it suffices me an hour' – the enough-thing is the subject, you're the object; fix the dangling 'Same reverse pattern' opener

target: Ils ont soif après le match.
english: They are thirsty after the game.
old: French says 'I have hunger' (`j'ai faim`), not 'I am hungry'. Same with `j'ai soif`, `j'ai froid`, `j'ai peur`, `j'ai 30 ans`. Sensations and age use `avoir`, not `être`.
focus: strip backticks; sensations take avoir – anchor with this card's 'ont soif' (they have thirst), keep the family list short

target: Nous avons faim après la randonnée.
english: We are hungry after the hike.
old: Watch these: faim, soif, chaud, froid, sommeil, peur, raison, tort, honte, de la chance. All take `avoir`. Saying `je suis faim` would mean you are hunger.
focus: strip backticks; keep the hook 'je suis faim would mean you ARE hunger', anchor with this card's 'avons faim', trim the ten-item list

english: Do you have a menu in English?
old: 'Avoir' in inversion: 'avez-vous des enfants?' Formal question form. 'Des' = some (partitive).
focus: inversion Avez-vous = the formal question form – use this card's 'Avez-vous un menu'; cut the 'des = partitive' bit (no des in this sentence)

target: Elle sort du bureau à cinq heures.
english: She leaves the office at five.
old: 'Sortir' = to go out/leave. Irregular -ir: je sors, il sort. 'Du' = de+le: 'sort du bureau' = leaves the office.
focus: keep only du = de + le: 'sort du bureau' = leaves the office – drop the sortir conjugation listing

old: `on` is the all-purpose informal 'we' in spoken French: `on va au cinéma` = 'we're going to the movies' (not `nous`). Verbs conjugate as 3rd singular even though it means 'we'.
focus: strip backticks; keep on = spoken-French 'we' with 3rd-singular verb – anchor with this card's 'on mange'

old: French says 'it makes' for weather: `il fait beau` (the weather's nice), `il fait froid`. Same pattern with `du soleil`, `du vent`. English uses 'be' or 'is sunny/windy'.
focus: Weather uses faire – 'il fait beau' is literally 'it makes nice'; quote this card, strip backticks, trim the extra examples.

old: French negation wraps the verb: `je ne sais pas`. In speech the `ne` often drops (`je sais pas`) but it stays in writing. `Pas` alone after the verb is colloquial.
focus: ne...pas wraps the verb, and spoken French often drops the ne – anchor to 'tu ne manges pas', strip backticks and the off-card example.

old: 'Vieux' has special forms: vieux (m. before consonant), vieil (m. before vowel), vieille (f.), vieux (m. pl.), vieilles (f. pl.).
focus: vieil is the special masculine form before a vowel – anchor to 'vieil homme', cut the five-form paradigm list.

target: À quelle heure tu te lèves ?
english: What time do you get up?
old: Reflexive verbs use a pronoun (me/te/se/nous/vous/se) before the verb. `Je m'appelle` = 'I call myself' = 'My name is'. The pronoun must match the subject.
focus: te lèves is literally 'you raise yourself' – reflexive pronoun must match the subject; quote this card, strip backticks and the m'appelle example.

target: Comment on va à la gare ?
english: How do we get to the station?
old: `on` also = English 'one' or 'they' (impersonal): `on dit que...` = 'they say that...'. Two meanings, one word. Context decides.
focus: on here is casual 'we' (on va) but also means 'one/they' – anchor to 'on va', strip backticks.

old: Possessives: ton/ta/tes (your, informal). Before feminine nouns starting with a vowel, use 'mon/ton/son' instead of 'ma/ta/sa': mon amie.
focus: ton matches frère's gender, not the owner's – French possessives track the noun; drop the off-card 'mon amie' exception.

old: More elisions: ne → n', me → m', te → t', se → s', le/la → l', de → d', que → qu'. Any vowel collision triggers it.
focus: One rule: de shrinks to d' before a vowel – quote 'besoin d'un stylo', cut the seven-item elision list.

old: 'Gros' (m.) → 'grosse' (f.) = big/fat. Multiple adjectives: size before noun + color after: un gros chien noir.
focus: Adjective placement is the insight – gros (size) before the noun, noir (color) after; one rule, drop the grosse form note.

target: Il y a du vent aujourd'hui.
old: 'Du/de la/des' for partial quantities: 'Je mange du pain' = I eat some bread (not all bread).
focus: Weather takes the partitive – 'du vent' is literally 'some wind'; anchor to this card, drop the 'je mange du pain' example.

target: Il y a trop de bruit.
old: `il y a` = 'there is / there are' – singular and plural. `Il y a une pomme`, `il y a trois pommes`. The form doesn't change. Past: `il y avait`.
focus: 'il y a' never changes for singular or plural – anchor to 'trop de bruit', strip backticks, cut the past-tense aside.

old: 'Beau' has special forms: beau (m. before consonant), bel (m. before vowel), belle (f.), beaux (m. pl.), belles (f. pl.).
focus: Cut the five-form list; hook the surprise that beau becomes bel before a vowel (un bel homme), anchored to 'un beau pays'.

old: When two BANGS adjectives are before a noun, the order is generally: size + other quality: un joli petit village, un grand beau jardin.
focus: Keep the both-adjectives-before-the-noun insight for 'un joli petit village'; drop the self-contradicting size-first claim and the unexplained BANGS jargon.
